content: Training materials are developed for specific categories of health workers, ensuring they are tailored to their roles and responsibilities. These materials are aligned with internationally applicable guidelines and standards, providing a consistent framework for health practices globally. Comprehensive reviews and analyses of health policies, programs, and research are conducted to ensure evidence-based approaches. Additionally, state-of-the-art consensus reports are created to offer technical advice and recommendations for decision-makers, ensuring informed and effective health interventions. These publications are closely linked to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) priority activities, which include the prevention and control of diseases, the development of equitable health systems grounded in primary health care, and the promotion of health for individuals and communities. Achieving better health for all requires the global dissemination and exchange of information, leveraging the collective knowledge and experience of WHO’s Member States and collaboration with world leaders in public health and biomedical sciences. To ensure the widest possible availability of authoritative health information, WHO facilitates the international distribution of its publications and encourages their translation and adaptation to local contexts. By promoting health, preventing disease, and controlling its spread worldwide, WHO’s publications contribute to the organization’s overarching goal: enabling all people to achieve the highest possible level of health. The WHO Technical Report Series disseminates findings from various international expert groups, providing the organization with the latest scientific and technical advice on a wide range of medical and public health topics. Members of these expert groups serve in their personal capacities without remuneration, and their views do not necessarily reflect the decisions or policies of WHO. Since the launch of the global framework to eliminate human rabies transmitted by dogs by 2030, WHO has collaborated with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the World Organisation for Animal Health, the Global Alliance for Rabies Control, and other stakeholders to develop a global strategic plan. This plan adopts a country-centric approach to empower and support national entities in controlling and eliminating rabies. WHO has convened its network of collaborating centers on rabies, specialized institutions, members of the WHO Expert Advisory Panel on Rabies, and other experts to review strategic and technical guidance for implementing country and regional programs. This report provides updated, evidence-based guidance on various aspects of rabies prevention, control, and elimination. Key updates include: 1. Surveillance strategies, including cross-sectoral system integration and appropriate diagnostics. 2. The latest recommendations on human and animal immunization. 3. Palliative care approaches in low-resource settings. 4. Risk assessment protocols to guide the management of bite victims. 5. A proposed process for validating and verifying countries that achieve zero human deaths from rabies. The meeting endorsed recommendations by the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) in October 2017 to improve access to affordable rabies biologics, particularly for underserved populations, and to enhance programmatic feasibility in alignment with the goals of universal health coverage. The collaborative mechanisms required to prevent rabies serve as a model for One Health collaboration at all levels, involving multiple stakeholders and ensuring coordinated efforts. Rabies is a vaccine-preventable disease, and providing support to countries will alleviate the pain and suffering caused by rabies, which disproportionately affects children. Investing in rabies control and elimination strengthens health systems, improves equity and access to healthcare, and contributes to sustainable development. Such investments not only aim to eliminate this fatal yet preventable disease but also build capacity in some of the world’s most neglected regions.
